acceptedReports.program: Perinatal mental-health training, access and peer support

acceptance.scope: Conditional finite training/peer component with signed household resources and explicit transfer/counterparty alternatives; not complete portfolio or verified marginal-gift EV.

what: Maternal Mental Health NOW trains health and social-service providers and offers culturally responsive perinatal peer support in LA County.
Its Sana Sana service provides weekly follow-up, resource navigation and free support groups; the organization became independent from Community Partners on July 1, 2025.
Through provider education and ongoing peer contact, it helps parents recognize distress and find appropriate support.
strengths: Better-equipped providers can identify distress and connect parents to appropriate clinical care.
Sana Sana offers ongoing, bilingual, affirming support rather than only a referral directory.
External randomized evidence supports plausible short-term clinical mechanisms, with uncertainty and differences in program intensity made explicit.
reservations: Training attendance and confidence do not establish completed care, patient caseload or causal health effects.
Current successor actual expenses and ordinary-gift expansion remain unverified; the transition return is not a full operating-cost measure.
Resource incidence, family spillovers and direct birthworker-transfer welfare are unmeasured; the combined price is a conditional partial reference.

sections.what: The [current mission and model](https://maternalmentalhealthnow.org/about-us/) combine provider training, stigma reduction and access to care. [Sana Sana](https://maternalmentalhealthnow.org/sana/) offers ongoing peer contact and resource navigation for LA County parents. The [FY25 impact report](https://maternalmentalhealthnow.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/MMHN-Impact-Report-FY25.pdf) dates independence from Community Partners to July 1, 2025; today’s gift is not a gift to all of the former sponsor’s projects.
sections.monitoring: The [donation page](https://maternalmentalhealthnow.org/donate/) reports 800+ trainees and 150 warmline callers during 2024–25. We do not add 300 support-group participants to callers because overlap and attendance definitions are unresolved. The [December 2025 Sana Sana white paper](https://maternalmentalhealthnow.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/MMHN-whitepaper-Dec2025-1.pdf) distinguishes repeated interactions from unique clients, reports low survey response, and describes weekly 30–60-minute support. Its billing projections are not actual reimbursement. Provider confidence and non-random differences between home-visitor and clinic screening are not causal health outcomes. Current fresh reporting confirms the counts but not deduplicated uptake or causal patient outcomes. The impact report additionally lists 500 warmline calls, which are not 500 unique parents, and $15,000 distributed to birthworkers, which is not earned income.
sections.qualitative: The [PoNDER economic analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6518383/) found a small adjusted six-month QALY gain from intensive UK health-visitor training in lower-risk postpartum women; uncertainty included no health gain. Our training model retains only 10% of that reference effect before further additionality and funding reductions. A [Canadian peer-support trial](https://www.bmj.com/content/338/bmj.a3064) found less probable depression at 12 weeks in high-risk women, but no significant difference at 24 weeks after referral of severe cases. It supports short-term benefit, not permanent remission. [LAMMHA’s funder report](https://www.chcf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/CollaborativeCareModelImprovesMaternalMentalHealth.pdf) identifies MMHN as training coordinator within a larger clinical coalition; all clinical outcomes cannot be assigned to MMHN. Only positive clinical contributions receive the cross-route overlap factor; negative clinical outcomes remain full. Peer 12-week endpoint improvement is translated with a finite, judged benefit-area assumption, not counted as lifetime remission. Clinical-null and adverse cases retain participant burdens. Existing LAMMHA grants and services are baseline.
sections.cost:
The [FY25 impact report](https://maternalmentalhealthnow.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/MMHN-Impact-Report-FY25.pdf), page 18, reports a $1.17 million operating budget. This is a full-program continuation-year planning cost, not audited actual spending or a verified marginal service queue. The original successor 990-EZ reports $1,513 pre-operating expenses while the operating program remained with Community Partners through June 30, 2025; no sponsor-wide budget or tiny transition cost is substituted. Actual sponsor transfers, all transition overhead and current reserves are unknown. Cost sensitivities use $1.0 million and $1.5 million; no comparable three-year full-recipient mean is available.

Central clinical benefit remains 0.4402119119 LA QALYs. Signed net resources subtract 0.2023741876 healthy-year welfare equivalents, giving 0.2378377243 combined equivalents and about $49.19 million per ten, versus the initial $26.58 million health-only reference. A $10,000 gift's modeled share gives 0.00376249 clinical QALYs and -0.00172969 income equivalents. These are linear capacity priors, not observed delivered outcomes per gift.

The resource ledger distinguishes 800 training records from a judged 80% unique course-user share and a separate 50% clinically effective frontline share. At 50% capacity response and 80% local residence, 256 local course users incur four hours at $25/hour, with 25% uncompensated: a net $25 own-household burden each at $60,000 baseline. Employer-paid training time and clinical backfill are separate unknown institutional costs, not counted again as participant lost wages. All course-user costs survive clinical failure.

The judged clinical-workflow resource exposure is 10% of the 12,000 annual care opportunities times funding response and geography: 480 local parent households incur $10 net time, travel or childcare cost. This exposure prior is distinct from the 10% clinical-effect transfer. The 75 incremental peer households incur $60 each. One participant per distinct household and one welfare person are modeled; family income and welfare are unpriced. Half of peer households are judged also exposed to clinical workflow: 37.5 joint households lose $70, 442.5 workflow-only lose $10 and 37.5 peer-only lose $60. Each household nets resources before the log; no separate same-household benefit logs. Course users and parent households are assumed disjoint, not observed disjoint; overlap across professional and parent roles remains an uncertainty.

All amounts are net after taxes, benefits, replacement care and foregone-work offsets by assumption, not measured expenditures. There is no central income gain. Resource-relief stresses add $100 net baseline-alive work or bill relief once per household, discount only that positive portion for 50% health overlap, and retain all negative costs. No survivor earnings, gross salary or gross billing is treated as welfare. One annual cohort and one household-resource year are counted after a one-year delay at 3%. A two-year stress explicitly assumes recurrent resource exposure, not measured persistence.

Private provider margin and insurer/public-payer net resources remain unknown, not factual zero; the central neutral anchor is partial-boundary bookkeeping. Separate stresses apply $500 net partner fiscal cost per reference-equivalent offer across 100 disjoint payer persons at $50,000 baseline, and ±$100 private margin across ten one-person owner households at $60,000 baseline. These are illustrative, not source-observed incidence. The external NHS £82 saving is not patient cash and is not converted into QALYs or subtracted from donor cost. The reported $15,000 Black Birthworker Enrichment Fund distributions establish a transfer, but unknown recipients, additionality, offsets and funding counterparties prevent a complete net-welfare estimate; it remains unpriced alongside other family and policy outcomes.

Direct-transfer stress explicitly uses the observed $15,000 Enrichment Fund aggregate, but not observed recipient net income. At 50% capacity response, 50% further causal transfer additionality and 10% taxes/benefit/opportunity offsets, twenty distinct one-person recipient households receive $168.75 net each before 50% positive health-overlap discount ($84.375). These shares, household count and $30,000 baseline are judgments. The matched hypothetical funding counterparty loses the full $3,750 incremental amount across 100 disjoint one-person households at $100,000 baseline; an adverse incidence case lowers that baseline to $20,000. These are alternative institutional funding/incidence hypotheses, not donor utility losses or proven public funding for this fund. Central transfer incidence stays unknown/unpriced, not zero evidence. The disjoint-recipient hypothesis is explicit; a half-overlap case instead assigns ten recipients to the modeled course cohort, removes their course-only pathways and jointly nets fund receipt with their full $25 course burden at the same $60,000 household baseline. No gross fund cash is counted on top of an overlapping household log. The reported three of eight peer participants training as birthworkers is not a causal placement or earnings result. Negative resource changes receive no positive overlap discount; sign-guard cases preserve full losses.
sections.funding: The FY25 operating-budget graphic attributes 55% to foundations/corporate, 25% government, 15% earned income and 5% individuals. Public and philanthropic support already finances delivery. The [current LAMMHA page](https://ccalac.org/los-angeles-maternal-mental-health-access-lammha/) describes the 2022–26 coalition program, closed enrollment and clinic implementation grants; these belong in the baseline. The [Sana Sana paper](https://maternalmentalhealthnow.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/MMHN-whitepaper-Dec2025-1.pdf) examines prospective billing, not guaranteed revenue, and [DHCS](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/medi-cal-peer-support-services/) confirms specialty-system peer support is a defined benefit rather than universal reimbursement for every peer interaction. Ordinary gifts may preserve uncovered capacity, replace other funding or fund administration; 50% marginal responsiveness is an explicit judgment. A post-transition budget, sponsor transfer reconciliation and cash runway would materially improve the estimate.

model.costScope: Full recipient program annual planning budget of $1.17m, not the $1,513 standalone pre-operation return and not former sponsor total. Modeled continuation year with current successor delivery assumed; actual full recipient expenses unverified. External clinical labor, insurer spending and participant time excluded from donor cost.
model.geographicAttribution: LA MSA is Los Angeles plus Orange counties. Sana Sana eligibility is LA County, so peer g=1. Training is available beyond LA and online; training beneficiary share .8 central (.5–.95) is judgment, not trainee/HQ location evidence. No global or state-policy spillovers added.
model.formula: QT=T*d*L*r*a*b*q; QP=P*peerUnique*e*rP*aP*b*u*w/52. Positive-only overlap H(x)=k*max(x,0)+min(x,0); QLA=[H(gT*QT)+H(QP)]/(1+discount)^delay. Course/resource exposure counts are independent of q/r clinical efficacy. Joint household signed net resources BEFORE log; income=.5*persons*discounted years*log(1+net/baseline). Price10=10*C/(QLA+income).
model.counterfactual: Current grants, commissioned training, other educators, clinical providers and referral services persist without the next ordinary gift. a and aP remove substitution by alternative training/support; b discounts donation-to-expanded/preserved service responsiveness. The 2022–26 LAMMHA grants and enacted screening laws are baseline, not fresh gift outcomes.
model.attribution: T is an output floor, d removes duplicate/non-frontline training records, L is a subjective annual unique lower-risk postpartum caseload per effective trainee, and r scales the intensive UK training reference to heterogeneous MMHN courses. Peer rP allows lower intensity and different risk profile than the high-risk RCT. k removes cross-route overlap. No additional LAMMHA, screening, group-attendance or awareness QALYs are layered onto these pathways.
model.uncertainty: Conditional partial estimate, not calibrated posterior or complete portfolio EV. External clinical uncertainty and all resource-incidence assumptions remain material. Complete unknown remains null; financial-only/clinical-null retains full household costs.
model.nativeOutcomes: Central annual modeled pipeline: 400 effective unique frontline trainees; 12,000 lower-risk care opportunities; 300 reference-equivalent training offers. Resource cohorts separately include 256 local course users, 480 workflow-exposed parents and 75 peer households, with 37.5 joint parent households. None is measured completed treatment. Clinical .4402119119 QALYs and signed income −.2023741876 equivalents.

historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: Current grants, commissioned training, other educators, clinical providers and referral services persist without the next ordinary gift. a and aP remove substitution by alternative training/support; b discounts donation-to-expanded/preserved service responsiveness. The 2022–26 LAMMHA grants and enacted screening laws are baseline, not fresh gift outcomes.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: T is an output floor, d removes duplicate/non-frontline training records, L is a subjective annual unique lower-risk postpartum caseload per effective trainee, and r scales the intensive UK training reference to heterogeneous MMHN courses. Peer rP allows lower intensity and different risk profile than the high-risk RCT. k removes cross-route overlap. No additional LAMMHA, screening, group-attendance or awareness QALYs are layered onto these pathways.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Best-effort partial-health scenario, heavily judgment-driven; no empirically measured MMHN causal conversion. Positive scenarios are not confidence bounds. Reference training QALY CI includes zero; negative case retained. Full policy, anti-stigma, workforce and infant/family outcomes are unpriced, not known to be absent.
historicalAlphaModel.nativeOutcomes: Central training pipeline: 800 records→400 effective unique frontline trainees→12,000 unique lower-risk postpartum care opportunities→300 reference-equivalent opportunities after transfer/additionality/funding. Peer pipeline: 150 callers→9.375 high-risk RCT-equivalent participants after transfer/additionality/funding→1.03125 fewer probable-depression cases at 12 weeks, translated with .1 utility×12/52 year. These are expected model quantities, not observed treated cases. No infant mortality or lifetime recurrence multiplier.

sensitivity: The positive low/high scenarios are stress tests, not calibrated probability quantiles; training caseload and clinical implementation dominate. Zero additional funding response yields zero benefit.

The original training Table 5 QALY difference is .002 with 95% CI−.001 to .004. Cost-saving probability is not a 99% probability of improved health; NHS cost savings are not subtracted from this donor numerator.

Training benefit ends at six-month follow-up for each modeled parent, with only one annual cohort. Peer benefit is .1 utility for 12 weeks per incremental probable-depression case; no persistence beyond 24 weeks assumed. The peer benefit area is a subjective scenario, not the trial's measured duration of improvement.

At the central $1.17m budget, $1m/10 requires 11.7 LA QALYs; $100k/10 requires 117. Central modeled component=.44021. With other factors fixed, training caseload would need about 835 lower-risk parents per effective trainee to approach $1m/10; do not treat that threshold as observed capacity.

Cost should be updated from reconciled current recipient accounts; $1,513 is not a cheaper valid scenario. Paid clinical follow-through is a necessary complementary resource and could materially raise societal costs.
